name: Pavalavannar Perumal Temple (Thiruppavalavannam), Kanchipuram
deity: Vishnu as Pavalavannar, the coral-hued Lord, with the Goddess Pavalavalli Thayar
period: A Divya Desam of Thondai Nadu, sung by Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
summary: At Thiruppavalavannam in Kanchipuram, Vishnu is worshipped as Pavalavannar, the coral-hued Lord, with Pavalavalli Thayar — a Divya Desam of Thondai Nadu sung by Thirumangai Alvar.

sections.history: Thiruppavalavannam is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu praised by the Alvars in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and it belongs to Thondai Nadu. Thirumangai Alvar sang the Lord of this shrine, and the tradition holds that Peyalvar and Thirumazhisai Alvar, too, celebrated the different forms of God worshipped within this temple. It stands in Kanchipuram, the ancient temple city, where a pilgrim can walk from one Divya Desam to the next. The name itself carries the devotion: Pavalavannar means the one whose hue is that of red coral, the colour in which the devotees have long seen their Lord.
sections.architecture: The sanctum houses Pavalavannar, and the Goddess is honoured as Pavalavalli Thayar, whose shrine stands in the outer prakaram together with that of Andal. North of the flagstaff are separate shrines for the Alvars, a reminder that this is a temple of the Divya Prabandham as much as of the image. The pillared courts and processional paths follow the familiar Dravidian plan of the Vaishnava temples of Kanchipuram.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of the sage Bhrigu, who set out to learn which of the three great deities, Brahma, Vishnu or Shiva, was supreme, and tested each in turn. At this place Vishnu appeared before the sage as Pavalavannar, the coral-hued Lord. The shrine therefore remembers a story of humility and patience: the Lord who receives the sage's test with grace, and shows his form to the seeker who has come in search of truth.
sections.festivals: Vaikunta Ekadashi is the great day of the Vaishnava year here, as at every Divya Desam, and the verses of the Divya Prabandham are recited on festival days, including those of Thirumangai Alvar. The temple also takes part in the festival life of Kanchipuram. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: A quiet, devotional visit rewards those who go slowly: the coral-hued Lord in the sanctum, the shrine of Pavalavalli Thayar and Andal in the outer prakaram, and the Alvars north of the flagstaff. Many pilgrims pair it with the nearby Pachaivannar shrine, the emerald-hued Lord, so that the two colours of Vishnu are seen on the same walk. Combine it with other Divya Desams of Kanchipuram.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; Vaikunta Ekadashi and festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in Kanchipuram, about 1.5 km from Kanchipuram railway station and about 2.5 km from the bus stand, so auto-rickshaws or a short walk suffice. Chennai, about 70 km to the north-east, is the nearest major airport.
